desc:
For a string s of length n, let z[i] be the length of the longest common prefix of s and the suffix s[i..n-1]. By definition z[0] = n. Return the sum z[0] + z[1] + ... + z[n-1].

For example, s = "ababa" has z = [5, 0, 3, 0, 1], so the answer is 9. For s = "aaa", z = [3, 2, 1] and the answer is 6.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
The answer is at most n(n+1)/2 and fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Computing each z[i] by comparing characters from scratch is O(n²) in the worst case, for example on a string of all equal letters.
Keep the rightmost segment [l, r) found so far that matches a prefix of s. For a position i inside it, s[i..r) equals s[i-l..r-l), so z[i] is at least min(r - i, z[i - l]).
Start from that lower bound and extend by direct comparison only while characters keep matching; update [l, r) whenever you extend beyond r. Finally sum the array.
editorial: The Z-algorithm computes the whole array in linear time. Maintain a window [l, r) with the largest right end among all segments s[i..i+z[i]) seen so far; this window is a copy of the prefix s[0..r-l).

For a new index i < r, the substring s[i..r) mirrors s[i-l..r-l), so z[i] starts at min(r - i, z[i - l]). For i ≥ r start from zero. Then extend with character comparisons while s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]. If the match reaches beyond r, move the window to [i, i + z[i]).

Every comparison that succeeds pushes r to the right, and r never moves back, so the total number of extension steps is at most n; the total running time is O(n). The sum for the maximum input (all equal letters) is 200,010,000, safely below 231.
